name: Centre for the Governance of AI (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: an AI catastrophe kills people everywhere and the future lost is everyone's, so the result is spread by world population.
summary: The Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI: a US charity with a UK subsidiary in London) researches how governments and AI companies can manage risks from advanced AI, advises them (in 2025 its director of policy was one of the chairs and vice-chairs who drafted the EU's Code of Practice for general-purpose AI) and trains people for the field (81 three-month fellows and 15 year-long scholars in 2025). This model covers all its work in 2025, its first full year as an independent charity ($11.9M spent, from its annual report; no audited statement for the year is public yet). At the defaults it averts about 1.6 years of healthy life per $1,000, from 0.05 to 33 on the model's own ranges, so the result is mostly uncertainty: each dollar of research is valued as a typical project's cut in the forecast risk of an AI catastrophe (Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's experts), the Code of Practice by GovAI's share of the resources behind it (about 1%) of a small cut in the risk (0.1%), the fellows' and scholars' later work at a typical dollar of such work, deaths valued like every death and the future lost counted through the discount rate; the research gives about half the result, the training two fifths and the Code a tenth, and the next dollar counts at 42% of the past average. It is close to the Center for AI Safety's and far above METR's, MIRI's and Redwood Research's mainly because a fifth of its catastrophe research is threat modelling of AI-enabled attacks, for which Rethink's typical misuse project cuts deaths far more per dollar than a misalignment one; the biggest swings are the chance of an AI catastrophe (the slider), the years a cut counts, the discount rate, that cut per dollar and the share of work counted as misuse, and every branch is discounted for missing data: no outcome of the work on the risk is measured.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

source.quote: In 2025, our total expenses for the year came to $11.9 million USD, growing by almost 100% compared to 2024.

rows.explainer: All of GovAI's spending in 2025, its first full year as an independent organisation (the US charity and its UK subsidiary together), every programme modelled: research, talent development (the Seasonal Fellowships, the Research Scholar programme, the Policy Program) and policy engagement. The annual report gives only total expenses ($11.9M, rounded), not a programme split, and no audited statement for 2025 is public yet (the US return for 2025 isn't filed; the UK subsidiary filed unaudited accounts without an income statement), so the total stands for the programmes with overhead spread alike. The only audited year, 2024, is a short first return of the new US entity ($919,661 spent, $380,976 on programmes) while most of that year's work ran elsewhere, so it can't be matched to the year's fellows and papers. The total includes 'one-off costs for the fit out of our new London office' (p. 18) in its 20% for facilities; the report doesn't say whether these are cash outlays or the year's depreciation (the UK subsidiary carries £3.6M of fixed assets written off over five years), so the low end takes about $1.2M off for fit-out serving later years.

rows.label: AI: share of the AI spending on work against misuse (threat modelling of AI-enabled attacks, chemical and biological evaluation standards)
rows.explainer: Of GovAI's research and policy work on catastrophic risk (the part counted, see catastrophe_relevant_share), the share aimed at people using AI to do harm. The Threat Modelling Team, set up in 2025, converts dual-use biological capability evaluations into risk estimates (Righetti, 'Dual-Use AI Capabilities and the Risk of Bioterrorism'), forecast LLM-enabled biorisk with the Forecasting Research Institute, wrote STREAM, a reporting standard for chemical and biological evaluations, and modelled AI attacks on the power grid, cybercrime, worms and chemical attacks (annual report pp. 5-6, 10); a CBRN seminar and CBRN grading standards add to it. That is about 4 to 5 of some 32 researchers and scholars, about 15% of research, or a fifth of the catastrophe-relevant part. The rest (frontier safety frameworks and third-party compliance reviews, regulation of frontier developers, compute thresholds, agent governance) is aimed at both misuse and loss of control and counts as misalignment work, as the family's rule says. 20%, our judgment, 10% (the publications alone: 3 of 28) to 35% (agent accountability and flaw disclosure counted as misuse too). The result moves almost in proportion with this share, because Rethink Priorities' typical misuse project cuts deaths in survivable catastrophes far more per dollar than its misalignment one.

source.quote: a multi-stakeholder consultation with almost 430 submissions

rows.explainer: GovAI's spending behind the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice (published 10 July 2025): Markus Anderljung, its director of policy and research, was vice-chair of Working Group 4 (internal risk management and governance of providers), one of the 13 chairs and vice-chairs (9 of them on the Safety and Security chapter), through the drafting rounds to the final text, with other staff giving expert input on the AI Act's scope through the Joint Research Centre (annual report p. 14). Perhaps a third to a half of one senior researcher's year plus some colleagues' time, with overhead, about $240,000, 2% of the year's spending, our estimate, 1% to 3%; left out of the AI field work so nothing counts twice.

source.title: European Commission, The General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
source.quote: The code was published on July 10, 2025.

rows.explainer: One standard adopted in 2025 that GovAI helped draft: the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, signed by 22 providers (Amazon, Anthropic, Google, IBM, Microsoft, Mistral AI, OpenAI and others; xAI its Safety and Security chapter only; Meta declined), which gives signatories a way to show they meet the AI Act's obligations for models with systemic risk.

rows.label: Policy win: chance it happens because of this work
rows.explainer: 1: the Code was won in the year (published 10 July 2025), so it happens for certain; GovAI's part of it is in cf_policy (what another expert in its seat wouldn't have written) and attr_policy (its share of the resources behind the chapter), as the template says for a win already in the year.

source.title: European Commission, The General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
source.quote: The code was published on July 10, 2025.

rows.label: Policy win: share of the area's yearly risk it removes while in force
rows.explainer: The share of the yearly AI catastrophe risk the Code's Safety and Security chapter removes while in force, beyond what the AI Act itself requires: Article 55 already obliges providers of models with systemic risk to evaluate and test them, assess and mitigate systemic risks, report serious incidents and secure them, and most signatories (most frontier developers serving the EU, Meta excepted) already had frontier safety frameworks under the 2024 Seoul commitments. The Code adds concrete, checkable commitments (a written safety and security framework, risk acceptance criteria, model reports to the AI Office, external evaluation in some cases), with enforcement from August 2026; models for other markets fall outside it. Anchors: Rethink Priorities' typical rate (at GovAI's mix a typical $1 million cuts about 0.001% of the yearly AI deaths risk and about 0.00008% of the extinction risk, so the chapter's resources, code_resources, would cut about 0.02% of the deaths risk and 0.002% of the extinction risk) and the family's default for a measure in force (1%, 0.1% to 5%). 0.1%, our judgment, between the two because detailed commitments that most frontier developers signed act more directly than a typical project; one cut for both sizes because the frameworks' thresholds cover loss of control as well as misuse, so it is 5 times a typical rate for the deaths risk and about 60 times for extinction; 0.01% (near a typical project's rate) to 0.5%.

source.quote: Recent data shows that about 60% of our alumni have settled into a longer-term role in AI governance a year after their fellowship ended

rows.explainer: Share of the fellows and scholars who go on to work on AI risk because of the programme. GovAI's alumni data: about 60% hold a longer-term AI governance role a year after the fellowship (scholars move on to the UK AI Security Institute, the Centre for Long-Term Resilience, Microsoft or stay as Research Fellows); its alumni survey (2024 Form 990, Part III) credits the fellowship with bringing careers forward by a year and raising alumni's future impact by 50%, so about a third of their later work. Most were selected from 18,000 applications and many would have entered the field anyway, and not every AI governance role is about catastrophic risk: 60% × about a third ≈ 20%, a little more with the scholars' year-long stays, 22%, our judgment, 8 to 40%, the family's 20% (5 to 40%) for selective fellowships.

source.quote: Another project team conducted a randomized controlled trial  assessing how retrieval-augmented generation and AI reasoning models could affect legal work

rows.explainer: Not all of GovAI's research is about catastrophes: its economics work (firms' exposure to language models, AI and legal work, the Department of Labor's AI workforce data, benefit sharing), US competitiveness (export promotion, data centres in the UAE) and public opinion surveys are about AI's economic and political effects, valued in unmodelled_benefits_adj, not through the catastrophe chances. By the 2025 output list (pp. 23-26) 11 of 37 items are of that kind (30%), but the frontier-risk teams (risk management, threat modelling, regulatory design) are larger than their paper counts: about 20% of research and policy spending, so 80%, our judgment, 65 to 90%.

rows.label: Research and policy: how far the typical project's effect applies to the catastrophe-relevant part

source.title: GovAI, Annual Report 2025 (published early 2026)
source.quote: Jonas Freund led a survey on thresholds for advanced AI systems in collaboration with the OECD, and we also hosted two secondees to the organization

rows.explainer: GovAI's catastrophe-relevant research and advice against Rethink Priorities' typical small AI project, the Code of Practice left out (it is the policy branch). Above typical: its work reaches where rules are made: two writers of the International AI Safety Report, secondees to the UK's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and the OECD, advice to frontier AI companies on designing their safety frameworks, a survey of thresholds run with the OECD. Below in how directly it acts: governance research cuts the risk only through what governments and companies then do, and much of it is analysis whose use isn't recorded. Net 1, a typical project, our judgment, 0.5 to 1.2 (the family's ceiling), between the Nuclear Threat Initiative's 0.8 and the Center for AI Safety's 1.2 for benchmarks the labs report.

rows.label: Field-building: how far the typical project's effect applies
rows.explainer: The fellows' and scholars' later work is already valued at a typical project's dollar of AI work (fb_work_dollars), with who would have got there anyway in fb_share_working, so 1, our judgment, 0.7 to 1.2: alumni placed in governments and frontier companies (the UK AI Security Institute, the US Senate, Google DeepMind) may do more than typical work, others less.

rows.label: How far the typical project's effect applies to this charity's work
rows.explainer: How far Rethink Priorities' typical small AI project applies to GovAI's work, branch by branch, weighted by each branch's healthy years (w_ai, w_fb, w_pol): the research and policy work at the share of it aimed at catastrophic risk times its uptake, the training at its own factor, and the Code of Practice at 1, its cut being judged directly (pol_relative_cut).
rows.formula: (w_ai * catastrophe_relevant_share * research_uptake_adj + w_fb * talent_evidence_adj + w_pol) / (w_ai + w_fb + w_pol)

rows.label: Research and policy: share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: Other groups do frontier AI governance research and advice (the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, RAND, the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, the Centre for Long-Term Resilience, the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, the AI Security Institutes and the companies' own policy teams); GovAI's threat models are less easily replaced. Our judgment, 0.6 (0.35 to 0.85), a little below the Center for AI Safety's 0.65 because AI governance is a more crowded field; that the work would have come years later is in years_of_impact.

rows.label: Field-building: share of the fellowship places no one else would have offered now
rows.explainer: Only whether another organisation would have run these fellowship and scholar places now: who would have reached the field anyway is already netted out in fb_share_working (from GovAI's alumni survey, which compares with the fellows' other options). Other governance fellowships (IAPS, ERA, Pivotal) are smaller and also oversubscribed (GovAI had 18,000 applications for 81 places), so few of these places would have been offered elsewhere: 0.9, our judgment, 0.75 to 1.

rows.label: Share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: The share of the work no one else would have done now, branch by branch: research and policy at cf_research, the training at cf_talent, the Code of Practice at cf_policy. Weighted by each branch's healthy years after evidence_adj, so that the product of the adjustments is each branch's own product.
rows.formula: (w_ai * catastrophe_relevant_share * research_uptake_adj * cf_research + w_fb * talent_evidence_adj * cf_talent + w_pol * cf_policy) / ((w_ai + w_fb + w_pol) * evidence_adj)

rows.label: Research and policy: GovAI's share of the resources behind its outputs

source.title: GovAI, Annual Report 2025 (published early 2026)
source.quote: Yoshua Bengio et al. (including GovAI researchers Sam Manning and Ben Garfinkel as writers)

rows.explainer: Many outputs are joint: the International AI Safety Report (led by Yoshua Bengio, GovAI two of its writers), the biorisk forecasts with the Forecasting Research Institute, STREAM and flaw disclosure with outside co-authors, the thresholds survey with the OECD; most reports are GovAI's own staff's. Our judgment, 75% (60% to 90%), as for the Center for AI Safety's research.

rows.label: Field-building: GovAI's share of the resources behind the training
rows.explainer: GovAI pays the fellows' and scholars' salaries, supervisors and office; outside speakers at the seminars and hosts of secondments give some time. Our judgment, 95% (85% to 100%), as for the Center for AI Safety's field-building. The alumni's employers' share is in fb_credit_share.

rows.label: Code of Practice: share of GovAI's contribution no one else in its seat would have made
rows.explainer: The AI Act required a code, so it would have existed without GovAI; the question is how much of GovAI's contribution to its text another expert as vice-chair would have made anyway. Reference class: the family's 0.7 (0.4 to 0.95) and the peers' 0.65 to 0.75 for whole organisations' work; a single seat that the Commission filled from many qualified candidates, on a text that followed the companies' existing frameworks and the plenaries' input, sits below them: about half, our judgment, 0.3 to 0.8 (an expert with less frontier-safety background in the seat).

rows.label: Code of Practice: everyone's resources behind the Safety and Security chapter (dollars)

source.title: European Commission, Meet the Chairs leading the development of the first General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
source.quote: a multi-stakeholder consultation with almost 430 submissions

rows.explainer: Everyone's spending and in-kind time behind the chapter, from July 2024 to July 2025: the AI Office's drafting and policy staff (about 20 people for a year, about $3M), the 13 chairs and vice-chairs (part-time for a year, about $1.3M), almost 430 written submissions (about $4M at a few weeks' work each), plenaries and workshops with about a thousand participants (about $3M), and the providers' own policy and safety teams negotiating the text (about $5-10M): about $20M, our judgment, $5M to $50M.

rows.label: Code of Practice: GovAI's share of the resources behind the Safety and Security chapter
rows.explainer: Credit by share of resources: GovAI's spending on the Code (pol_cost_share of its cost, about $240,000: its vice-chair's time and colleagues' input) over everyone's resources behind the chapter (code_resources): about 1.2%. Counting heads (1 of the chapter's 9 chairs and vice-chairs, 11%) would overstate it, because the AI Office, the submitters and the providers did most of the work.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: GovAI's share of the resources behind its outputs, branch by branch: research and policy at attr_research, the training at attr_talent, the Code of Practice at attr_policy. Weighted by each branch's healthy years after the earlier adjustments, as Redwood Research's model chains them, so that the product of the adjustments is each branch's own product.
rows.formula: (w_ai * catastrophe_relevant_share * research_uptake_adj * cf_research * attr_research + w_fb * talent_evidence_adj * cf_talent * attr_talent + w_pol * cf_policy * attr_policy) / ((w_ai + w_fb + w_pol) * evidence_adj * counterfactual_adj)

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Whether its large funders (Coefficient Giving, formerly Open Philanthropy, the Survival and Flourishing Fund, Longview Philanthropy) would give less if small donors gave more is the room factor of @next_dollar.govai (docs/normalization.md 2.10), so it isn't asked again here (one question per adjustment): 1, our judgment, as for every catastrophic-risk model; 0.85 to 1.05 for funging the room factor misses.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no outcome of GovAI's work on the risk is measured, every branch rests on a typical project's effect and on judgment, so $missing_data_discount.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Good beyond the catastrophes counted: the economics and labour-market research (about a fifth of research, left out of the catastrophe chain by catastrophe_relevant_share) informs policy on AI's effects on jobs and growth; threat models also guard against attacks far smaller than a catastrophe (the bioterrorism report puts an AI-enabled rise in lone-wolf epidemic risk at about 12,000 expected deaths a year); the Policy Program (16 completed), the mentorship pilot, the London office's events and visitors, and safety-framework advice that also cuts everyday harms. 15% (5 to 35%) of the modelled value, our judgment, above the Center for AI Safety's 10% for the economics work.

rows.label: Harm: speeding up dangerous capabilities, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire (in the shared cut): governance work rarely advances capabilities, but GovAI's US policy work aims to help AI be 'developed quickly and adopted widely' (export promotion, building US data centres), and some alumni join frontier companies. -2%, our judgment, down to -10%, below the Center for AI Safety's -5% because GovAI builds no capability benchmark.

rows.label: Harm: information hazards and attention, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire: the Threat Modelling Team publishes assessments of how AI could help attackers (bioterrorism, the power grid, cybercrime, worms), which can draw bad actors' attention to a path; they estimate risk rather than give instructions and are reviewed before release. -3%, our judgment, down to -10%, between the Center for AI Safety's 0 to -5% for a benchmark of hazardous knowledge and FAR.AI's -5% for working attacks.
